title: He wept over the city (Luke 19:41–48)
hookLine: coming near Jerusalem, he weeps: if only you knew the things of peace

lines: IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SINGING.
cards: Coming down the Mount of Olives today, the road bends, and suddenly Jerusalem is laid out across the valley: walls, domes, towers, the old city glowing gold in the late light. People stop and take photos.
Luke says that when Jesus reached that point, in the middle of the singing crowd, he looked at the city. And he did something nobody around him expected on a day of celebration.

teach.h: HE BEHELD THE CITY, AND WEPT.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it."
Not quiet tears. At Lazarus's tomb in John's Gospel, the word is gentler: he shed tears. Here Luke uses the word for weeping aloud, sobbing, in the middle of the parade.
Then he speaks to the city as if it were a person he loves: "If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes."
Tradition hears the word for peace, shalom, in Jerusalem's name.

teach.h: THE THINGS THAT MAKE FOR PEACE.
teach.b: The city of peace, not knowing the things that make for peace. He describes enemies surrounding it, walls thrown down, "because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation." A visitation is God coming close.
Later, Roman armies did besiege Jerusalem and destroy the temple, and some Christians read these words as Jesus foreseeing it. But notice what he does with what he sees.
He doesn't gloat or threaten. He weeps, the way a parent grieves a child walking toward danger. And the weeping leads to action.
He goes into the temple and drives out the sellers: "My house is the house of prayer."

teach.h: IF THOU HADST KNOWN, EVEN THOU.
teach.b: Then he teaches there daily. The leaders want to destroy him, Luke says, but can't, because "all the people were very attentive to hear him." Tears, then a cleansing, then teaching.
Love for a city does all three.

how: On the Mount of Olives, the small church of Dominus Flevit, Latin for the Lord wept, marks the traditional spot, and Christians around the world pray for the peace of Jerusalem and of cities in conflict, often using the words of Psalm 122.

o: a friendly social call between neighbors

Jesus wept only once in the Gospels

he grieves: "if thou hadst known, even thou... the things which belong unto thy peace!"

games.q: the crowd is singing, the road bends, and Jerusalem lies before Jesus, the city where he'll be rejected. what does he do?
o: he raises his hands and joins the singing.
he weeps aloud over the city.
games.why: "when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it." in the middle of the parade, he sobs.

practice: Bring to mind a city where there's fighting or deep division right now, near or far, even your own town, and picture it from a hillside: the rooftops, the streets, the ordinary people inside.
Let yourself feel something for them, even grief.

If you pray, you can use the psalm's words, Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee, then ask in your own words for peace in the city you're picturing; if not, hold it in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Visitation: God coming close. Weeping, Jesus says Jerusalem didn't know the time of its visitation.

orig.note: Greek: he wept aloud, he sobbed. stronger than John's word for Jesus' tears at Lazarus's tomb.

carryVoice: Your line: if only you knew. He grieved before he did anything else. See you tomorrow.
